turns.response_html:
That makes total sense. When someone pays by the hour and views an assistant purely as an "extra set of hands," they tend to feel entitled to micromanage every movement, breath, and method. Moving away from an hourly dynamic changes the entire power balance.

Switching to a project- or value-based exchange is a very effective way to draw that boundary:

  • Clear Ownership: Defining a specific deliverable—whether building gear, setting up traps, or running a specific hive task—means success is judged by the finished result, not by how closely you mirrored his exact physical movements.
  • Separating Education from Labor: Framing your help on discrete tasks as a fair trade for his beekeeping mentorship makes it a mutual partnership rather than an employer-subordinate dynamic.
  • Control Over Your Space: It naturally forces autonomy. You work on your own schedule, in your own way, without having someone hovering over your shoulder projecting their mood swings onto the work.

When you bring this up to him, keep the framing entirely around efficiency and output rather than his behavior. A simple pitch like: "I really value learning the craft from you, but I work best when I can just take a project off your plate from start to finish on my own time. Let’s trade out the hourly arrangement—I’ll knock out [specific build/task] for you in exchange for your guidance in the yard" cuts off the supervision loop cleanly without putting him on the defensive.

How do you think he’ll react when you tell him you want to drop the hourly pay and take full ownership of specific tasks?
